drills.q: Why do refresh tokens exist at all instead of just issuing long-lived access tokens directly?
drills.a: Splitting tokens keeps the frequent hot-path operation (access-token verification on every request) stateless and lookup-free, while concentrating server-side state -- and therefore revocability -- into the infrequent refresh operation. A single long-lived access token needs either no revocation lever or a per-request lookup that defeats the point of statelessness.

drills.q: What does refresh token rotation mean precisely, and why isn't rotation alone sufficient security?
drills.a: Every refresh mints a new token and invalidates the one presented, limiting each token string to one use. But if an attacker has a copy and uses it before the legit client, they simply get the next valid token in the chain -- rotation alone doesn't detect this, it just relocates the theft window rather than closing it.

drills.q: In a rotation race between a legitimate client and an attacker holding a stolen copy, who actually gets locked out?
drills.a: Whichever party's refresh request the server processes SECOND gets rejected, since the first to arrive rotates the token and invalidates it for the other -- meaning the legitimate user could be the one locked out while the attacker keeps the valid chain, unless reuse detection revokes the whole family.

drills.q: Why does reuse detection require revoking the ENTIRE token family rather than just the specific reused token?
drills.a: Since every subsequent token in the chain descends from the same original grant, you can't be certain which specific token the attacker currently holds or has already used. Revoking only the flagged token leaves the rest of a potentially compromised chain still valid -- family-wide revocation is what actually contains the incident.

drills.q: A mobile app occasionally logs users out on flaky networks, and the team suspects rotation is the cause. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: A retried refresh request (client resends after a timeout, unaware the first succeeded) presents an already-rotated token a second time, indistinguishable from theft without a grace window, triggering family revocation and logout. Fix: a short (few-second) grace window that returns the same already-issued pair for a same-token retry.

drills.q: Give the exact worst-case exposure window after a security team decides to cut off a compromised account, in the access/refresh hybrid.
drills.a: Exactly the access token's TTL. Revoking the refresh token stops new access tokens from being minted, but any already-issued access token keeps working until its own exp regardless of the revocation action -- a 10-minute TTL means a real 10-minute worst case, independent of how fast the revocation itself executes.

drills.q: A colleague wants to store the refresh token in localStorage because it's simpler than handling cookie flags. Response?
drills.a: localStorage is fully JS-readable, so any successful XSS anywhere in the app's dependency tree can exfiltrate the token wholesale for offline, unlimited reuse. An httpOnly cookie removes that exfiltration path at the cost of reopening CSRF, which is well-mitigated with SameSite plus an anti-CSRF token -- the tradeoff favors cookies for anything sensitive.

drills.q: Does storing a token in an httpOnly cookie fully solve the XSS problem?
drills.a: No -- a live XSS payload can still ride the httpOnly cookie to make authenticated requests as the user while it's executing; it just can't copy the raw token for later separate reuse. This bounds blast radius to the payload's active execution window but doesn't replace closing the XSS vulnerability itself.

drills.q: Design a token lifecycle for a system where permission changes must take effect within 60 seconds per a compliance requirement.
drills.a: Rather than force a sub-60s access-token TTL (too aggressive for most refresh volumes), decouple authorization state from token TTL: cache permission lookups with a TTL matched to 60s or invalidate explicitly on permission-change events, and re-check current permissions server-side at the point of sensitive actions rather than trusting an embedded role claim.

drills.q: What does DPoP add beyond rotation with reuse detection?
drills.a: Reuse detection is detective -- it identifies theft only after a race between legit client and attacker, and whichever loses gets flagged (possibly the legit user). DPoP is preventive: the token is bound to a client-held private key via a signed per-request proof, so a stolen token without the key can't be used at all, regardless of any race.

drills.q: A security review finds refresh tokens with a 90-day TTL and no rotation. How do you prioritize the fix, and what about tokens already issued?
drills.a: Add rotation with reuse detection first -- the highest-value fix, converting an indefinitely-reusable leaked credential into one usable at most once per cycle with active theft detection. For tokens issued before the fix, either force a one-time re-login for all active sessions at deploy time, or explicitly accept they retain full original blast radius until natural expiry under the old TTL -- a tradeoff to state explicitly, not silently absorb.

drills.q: Compare: (a) short access-token TTL with no refresh rotation vs (b) longer access-token TTL with full rotation and reuse detection. Which is better and why?
drills.a: (a) bounds each access token tightly but leaves a stolen refresh token silently valid and reusable for its whole long lifetime with zero detection. (b) accepts a slightly longer access-token exposure per compromise but converts refresh-token theft from silent-and-long-lived into detected-on-next-use-and-contained. Choose (b): it fixes the more consequential, less-bounded failure mode (refresh-token theft), and in practice you'd combine both anyway.
